set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which four cell types make up the epidermis, and which predominates?
opts: Keratinocytes, melanocytes, Merkel cells and Langerhans cells, with keratinocytes about 90 percent
Correct. Because keratinocytes dominate so heavily, most epidermal pathology is fundamentally a keratinocyte problem.
Fibroblasts, macrophages, adipocytes and mast cells, with fibroblasts predominating
Those are dermal cells; the dermis is where fibroblasts and mast cells live.
Melanocytes, Merkel cells, fibroblasts and histiocytes, with melanocytes predominating
Fibroblasts and histiocytes are dermal, and melanocytes are a minority population.
Keratinocytes and melanocytes only, in roughly equal proportion
Four cell types are named, and the proportions are far from equal.

set1.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: A nodule is greater than 5 millimetres. What tissue does it arise from?
opts: Superficial epidermis only, with no dermal involvement
A nodule is defined by its dermal and subcutaneous depth.
Fluid accumulating between epidermis and dermis
That describes a bulla.
Dilated superficial dermal capillaries with no inflammatory infiltration at all
That is telangiectasia.
Dermal-based tissue with dense collagen bundles, extending into subcutaneous tissue
Correct. Epidermoid cysts are keratin-filled, dermatofibroma is fibrous tissue, and a rheumatoid nodule is fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by histiocytes.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Henoch-Schonlein purpura involves which systems, and which patients?
opts: The skin alone, with no systemic involvement whatsoever, at any age at all
The whole point of naming it is that it is systemic.
Skin, joints, kidneys and intestines, commonly in children aged 3 to 10 years
Correct — an immunoglobulin A vasculitis, which is why it is not confined to the skin.
Skin and lungs only, commonly in older adults
Neither the organs nor the age group match.
Skin and liver, commonly in neonates
Those organs and that age group are not described.

set1.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: How do hypertrophic scars and keloids depart from normal healing?
opts: Keratinocyte division slows and elastin degrades, thinning the tissue
That is atrophy, the opposite direction of change.

The inflammatory phase never resolves, so granulation tissue never forms at all and the wound remains open indefinitely without ever progressing to the proliferative or remodelling phases that normally follow
The problem is a prolonged proliferative phase, not an absent one.
Type I collagen is replaced by weaker type III in basket-weave orientation
That reverses the normal remodelling swap and is not the keloid mechanism.

Fibroblast dysregulation prolongs the proliferative phase, collagen deposition and degradation become imbalanced during remodelling, and collagen bundles develop haphazardly and exceed the boundaries of the initial wound
Correct. Two phases go wrong, and exceeding the original wound margin is the defining outcome.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: What produces leukonychia, and what else can cause it?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed
That is Terry's nails.
Increased capillary density with release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the nail bed tissue itself
That is clubbing.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed, usually harmless nail bed damage but also seen with heavy metal poisoning
Correct — white streaks or spots, also called Mee's lines.
A halt of keratin production, associated with illness and malnourishment
That is Beau's lines, which are transverse grooves.

set1.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What happens during the inflammatory phase of wound healing, and over what period?
opts: Days 1 to 3: type I collagen is laid down in basket-weave orientation
Collagen replacement belongs to remodelling, much later.
Days 1 to 3: a fibrin haemostatic plug forms, neutrophils and macrophages remove dead tissue, and growth factors and cytokines are secreted to signal the next phase
Correct. The phase both cleans the wound and issues the signal that starts proliferation.
Days 4 to 21: granulation tissue forms, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells that rebuild the wound bed from below over three weeks
That is the proliferative phase.
Days 21 to one year: type III collagen is replaced by type I
That is the remodelling phase.

set1.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: What distinguishes a vesicle from a bulla, mechanistically as well as by size?
opts: A vesicle is up to 5 millimetres with fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or directly beneath the epidermis; a bulla is greater than 5 millimetres and involves separation of epidermis from dermis
Correct. The bulla represents a deeper plane of cleavage, not merely a bigger blister.

A vesicle is greater than 5 millimetres and a bulla is up to 5 millimetres in diameter, and the two share an identical mechanism of fluid accumulation entirely within the epidermis rather than beneath it
The sizes are reversed and the mechanisms differ.
A vesicle is solid and a bulla is fluid-filled
Both are fluid-filled lesions.
A vesicle contains purulent material and a bulla contains serous fluid
Purulent content defines a pustule.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Eczematous dermatitis results from which type of inflammatory reaction?
opts: T cell-mediated
Correct — a chronic condition with frequent or infrequent flares, known as the itch that rashes.
Immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation alone
That is the urticaria mechanism.
Neutrophil-driven suppurative inflammation
That would produce pustules.
Complement-mediated vessel destruction
That describes a vasculitis.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which dermal cell mediates immunoglobulin E-mediated inflammation?
opts: The mast cell
Correct, and its degranulation is the mechanism behind both the wheal and urticaria.
The fibroblast
Fibroblasts produce collagen.
The melanocyte
Melanocytes produce pigment and sit in the epidermis.
The keratinocyte
Keratinocytes form the bulk of the epidermis and produce keratin.

set1.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: How are dermatofibroma and lipoma characterised in the tissue?
opts: Dermatofibroma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes; lipoma is a fibrous tissue overgrowth within the dermis
This reverses the two lesions.
Both are malignant proliferations of keratinocytes
Both are described as benign, and neither arises from keratinocytes.
Dermatofibroma is keratin-filled and lipoma is fluid-filled
Keratin filling describes an epidermal inclusion cyst.
Dermatofibroma is a benign overgrowth of fibrous tissue in the dermis; lipoma is a benign enclosed capsule of adipocytes
Correct. Both sit under the general term tumor, which describes rapid cellular growth and may or may not be malignant.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What are the two connective tissue layers of the dermis?
opts: Basale and spinosum
Those are epidermal layers.
Corneum and lucidum
Those are also epidermal layers.
The papillary and the subcutaneous, being the superficial and the deepest layers
The subcutaneous layer, or hypodermis, is the third layer of skin rather than part of the dermis.
Papillary, the thin superficial layer, and reticular, the dense deeper layer
Correct. The dermis is also where the blood vessels and mechanoreceptors sit.

set1.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What defines a secondary skin lesion?
opts: Any lesion that arises from malignant rather than from benign underlying disease processes
Neither category implies anything about malignancy.
A modification or change of a primary lesion caused by infection, trauma or other factors
Correct, which is why a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble what it came from.
Any lesion appearing on a second body site after the first
Location has nothing to do with the classification.
Any lesion that is palpable rather than flat
Palpability separates macules from papules within the primary group.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: What causes petechiae, and what size defines them?
opts: Mast cell histamine release with plasma leakage, up to 5 millimetres
That produces a wheal, which is transient and blanchable.
Minor bleeding into the dermis from capillary rupture, infection, thrombocytopenia or vasculitis, 1 to 2 millimetres or less
Correct, and they are non-blanchable because the blood sits outside the vessel rather than within it.
Permanent dilatation of the superficial dermal vessels, measuring 1 to 2 millimetres across the surface of the skin
That is telangiectasia, which blanches and involves no extravasated blood.
Increased melanin production in the basal layer, up to 5 millimetres
That produces a hyperpigmented macule.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which signalling pathway does basal cell carcinoma overactivate, and in which cells?
opts: The Hedgehog signalling pathway, following ultraviolet-induced mutation of basal keratinocytes in the epidermis
Correct. It is the most common skin cancer and the most common malignancy in humans, slow growing and rarely metastasising.
The tp53 tumour suppressor pathway, acting in the differentiated keratinocytes of the epidermis
That is squamous cell carcinoma.
Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, in immature keratinocytes
That is implicated in seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign.
Uninhibited melanocyte growth at the dermal-epidermal junction
That is melanoma.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the pathophysiology of actinic keratosis, and what does it carry a higher risk of?
opts: Benign proliferation of immature keratinocytes, carrying a higher risk for basal cell carcinoma of the head and neck region in later life especially
Benign immature keratinocyte proliferation describes seborrhoeic keratosis.
Human papillomavirus infection of basal cells, carrying higher risk for melanoma
That is verrucae vulgaris, and it does not lead to melanoma.
Autoimmune T cell infiltration, carrying higher risk for lymphoma
No such mechanism is described here.
Damage from excessive cumulative ultraviolet exposure leading to intraepidermal proliferation of dysplastic keratinocytes, carrying higher risk for squamous cell carcinoma
Correct — it is described as the most common precancer, which is exactly why the dysplasia matters.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: How do petechiae, purpura and ecchymoses differ?
opts: By size — petechiae 1 to 2 millimetres or less, purpura 3 to 10 millimetres, ecchymoses greater than 10 millimetres — with similar underlying pathology
Correct. It is a single process of bleeding into the dermis described at three scales.
By mechanism — petechiae from capillary rupture, purpura from vessel dilatation, and ecchymoses from melanin deposition in the dermis rather than blood
The pathology is described as similar across all three.
By depth — petechiae epidermal, purpura dermal, ecchymoses subcutaneous
All involve blood in the dermis; the distinction given is size.
By blanchability — petechiae blanch, purpura and ecchymoses do not
All three are non-blanchable.

set1.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set1.q: What distinguishes a primary from a secondary skin lesion?
opts: A primary lesion is the one that appears first in time, and a secondary lesion is any lesion that appears later at a different site elsewhere on the body
The distinction is about modification, not location or sequence of appearance.
A primary lesion is the direct result of the underlying disease and retains its original unmodified appearance; a secondary lesion has been modified over time
Correct, and a secondary lesion may or may not still resemble the lesion it came from.
A primary lesion is palpable and a secondary lesion is flat
Palpability separates macules from papules within the primary group; it is not the primary-versus-secondary distinction.
A primary lesion is benign and a secondary lesion is malignant
Neither category carries any implication about malignancy.

set1.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What is a fissure, and what conditions produce one?
opts: A thickened plaque produced by chronic rubbing
That is lichenification.
A dilated superficial vessel without inflammatory infiltrate
That is telangiectasia.
A linear ulcer forming a crack in the epidermis, from loss of elasticity or flexibility, severe dryness and mechanical tension, with hyperkeratosis thickening the stratum corneum
Correct. It is a linear form of ulceration rather than a distinct process.
A superficial loss of the epidermis that spares the dermal-epidermal junction and everything beneath it, so no collagen is ever destroyed in the process of healing
That is an erosion, and it is not linear by definition.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which tinea subtype affects the nails, and what is its other name?
opts: Tinea barbae, affecting nails and beard
Tinea barbae affects the beard area.
Tinea unguium, also called onychomycosis
Correct. Corporis is trunk and limbs, pedis foot, cruris groin, capitis head, facialis face, manuum hand, barbae beard.
Tinea capitis, also called onychomycosis
Tinea capitis affects the head.
Tinea manuum, affecting the nails of the hand
Tinea manuum affects the hand rather than the nails specifically.

set1.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What tissue makes up a scale?
opts: Focal loss of epidermis and dermis with destruction of the collagen beneath
That is an ulcer.
A compact portion of desquamating stratum corneum, varying in size and thickness
Correct, and psoriasis is the example given — which follows from its epidermal hyperplasia and loss of the granular layer.
Dried sebum, cellular debris, blood or necrotic skin
That is a crust.
Thickened epidermis induced by long-term scratching
That is lichenification.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Where does each step of vitamin D activation take place, beginning in the skin?
opts: Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin under ultraviolet B light, then hydroxylated first in the liver and then in the kidneys to the active form calcitriol
Correct. The skin only starts the process; two further hydroxylation steps in separate organs are needed before the hormone is active.
Calcitriol is produced directly in the skin under ultraviolet B light and requires no further modification in either the liver or the kidneys at all
The skin produces cholecalciferol, which is inactive until hydroxylated twice elsewhere.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the liver, then hydroxylated in the skin and finally in the kidneys
This reverses the order; production begins in the skin.
Cholecalciferol is produced in the skin and hydroxylated entirely within the kidneys in a single step
Two organs are involved in activation, the liver first and then the kidney.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which structural epidermal changes occur in psoriasis?
opts: Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with fluid accumulating between the two layers of the skin itself
That is a bulla.
Loss of melanocytes from the basal layer
That produces vitiligo.
Epidermal hyperplasia, loss of the stratum granulosum, and failure of epidermal cells to secrete lipids producing xeroderma
Correct. Losing the granular layer is what leaves the characteristic scale.
Thinning of the epidermis with slowed keratinocyte division
That is atrophy, the opposite direction of change.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: What defines telangiectasia at the tissue level?
opts: Dense inflammatory infiltration around dilated vessels
The lecture states specifically that there is no inflammatory infiltration.
Proliferation of new vessels driven by release of vascular endothelial growth factor into the surrounding dermis over a prolonged period
That mechanism is described for nail clubbing.
Permanent dilatation and thinning of the endothelium of capillaries, venules and arterioles in the superficial dermis, with NO inflammatory cell infiltration
Correct. The absence of inflammatory infiltrate is the discriminating feature.
Capillary rupture with blood deposited into the dermis
That produces petechiae and purpura.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What is sebum primarily composed of?
opts: Water, sodium and chloride electrolytes
That is eccrine sweat.
Keratin and keratohyalin
Those are epidermal structural proteins.
Collagen and elastin
Those are dermal structural proteins.
Triglycerides, wax esters and squalene
Correct, produced by the sebaceous glands associated with hair follicles to lubricate skin and hair.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the site of cellular division?
opts: The granular layer, known as the stratum granulosum
That layer contains keratohyalin granules and sits above the dividing layer.
The stratum lucidum
That is 2 to 3 layers of flattened dead keratinocytes.
The basal layer, or stratum basale, the deepest layer
Correct. A single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes, which also contains melanocytes and Merkel cells.
The stratum corneum, the outermost layer
The stratum corneum is 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes; nothing divides there.

set1.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set1.q: What happens to collagen during the remodelling phase, and how does the result differ from normal dermis?
opts: Type III collagen is replaced with stronger type I collagen oriented in small parallel bundles, whereas normal dermis has a basket-weave orientation
Correct. The scar is strong but architecturally different, which is why it never quite matches the surrounding skin.
Type I collagen is replaced with weaker type III collagen oriented in a basket-weave pattern throughout the scar tissue that results
This reverses both the collagen types and the resulting orientation.
Collagen is degraded entirely and replaced by elastin
Elastin is not the replacement fibre in scar remodelling.
Collagen production continues to increase indefinitely
The lecture notes that formation of granulation tissue ceases in this phase.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: Which hair type is regulated by androgens, and which grows independently of them?
opts: All three types are equally androgen-dependent
The lecture distinguishes them specifically on androgen regulation.
Terminal hair is androgen-regulated; vellus hair grows independently of androgens
Correct. Lanugo is the third type, the fine hair of newborns.
Vellus hair is regulated by androgens; terminal hair grows independently of them
This reverses the two.
Lanugo hair is androgen-regulated; terminal hair is not
Lanugo is newborn hair and is not the androgen-dependent type.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does human papillomavirus produce a common wart?
opts: It triggers mast cell degranulation in the dermis
That is the urticaria mechanism.
It digests keratin using keratinases and proteases
That is how dermatophytes behave.
It invades epidermal basal cells through microabrasions, leading to proliferation of the epidermis
Correct, and clinical variants of warts are often associated with distinct viral subtypes.
It infects the melanocytes that lie along the dermal-epidermal junction within the epidermis
That is where melanoma arises, and it is not viral.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which gene mutation is named for squamous cell carcinoma, and which histological features are pathognomonic?
opts: Overactivation of the Hedgehog pathway, with pearly papules and telangiectasias
Those describe basal cell carcinoma.
Activating mutation of fibroblast growth factor receptor-3, with a stuck-on waxy and scaly appearance on the skin
That is seborrhoeic keratosis, which is benign.
Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance and radial growth
Those features are described for melanoma.
Mutation in the tp53 tumour suppressor gene, with keratin pearls and epithelial pearls as pathognomonic features
Correct. It derives from keratinocytes, and immunosuppression is a notable risk factor.

set1.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set1.q: Why does psoriatic skin become dry, in the lecture's account?
opts: The stratum corneum is lost entirely
The granular layer is lost; the scale that remains is stratum corneum.
Sebaceous glands overproduce sebum, which dries the surface
Excess sebum relates to seborrhoeic dermatitis, and it does not dry the skin.
Epidermal cells fail to secrete lipids, producing xeroderma
Correct — the dryness follows from a secretory failure rather than from water loss alone.
Eccrine sweat glands are destroyed by inflammation
Sweat gland destruction is not described in psoriasis.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which receptors does the lecture name for the sensations of touch and pressure?
opts: Golgi tendon organs and muscle spindles
Those are proprioceptive receptors of muscle and tendon, not of skin.
Langerhans cells and melanocytes
Langerhans cells are immune sentinels and melanocytes produce pigment; neither is a mechanoreceptor.
Meissner's corpuscles, Pacinian corpuscles and Merkel cells
Correct. Meissner's serve fine discriminative touch and low-frequency vibration, Pacinian respond to deep pressure and vibration, and Merkel cells serve light touch.
Ruffini endings, Krause bulbs and free nerve endings only
Free nerve endings are named for touch, pain and temperature, but the three receptors listed for touch and pressure are different.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What are the two phases of allergic contact dermatitis?
opts: Irritation, then hyperkeratosis of the stratum corneum
That describes irritant contact dermatitis and lichenification respectively.
Radial growth, then vertical growth
Those are the growth phases of melanoma.

Sensitization, in which Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells to create specialised memory; and elicitation, in which re-exposure to the same hapten promotes T cell migration and cutaneous inflammation
Correct — a delayed hypersensitivity reaction occurring 48 to 72 hours after exposure. Nickel and poison ivy are the examples.
Sensitization by mast cell degranulation, followed by elicitation through the release of histamine into the surrounding dermal tissue on every subsequent exposure to that same allergen thereafter
That is the immunoglobulin E pathway of urticaria, not the T cell pathway here.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the main pathologic finding in nail clubbing, and what mediates it?
opts: Incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
That is leukonychia.
Increased capillary density, with increased release of vascular endothelial growth factor
Correct, and it is associated with lung, cardiovascular, liver and inflammatory bowel disease.
Overgrowth of the connective tissue within the nail bed itself over a period of time
That is Terry's nails.
A halt of keratin production at the matrix
That is Beau's lines.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which cells drive psoriasis, and which cytokines does the lecture name?
opts: Melanocytes proliferate at the dermal-epidermal junction
That is the origin of melanoma.
Active T cells infiltrating the epidermis stimulate keratinocyte proliferation and excessive cytokine production, particularly tumour necrosis factor alpha, interferon gamma and interleukin-12
Correct. It is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory dermatosis, and skin cells multiply up to ten times faster than normal.
Mast cells release histamine which drives keratinocyte proliferation
That is the urticaria pathway and does not produce psoriasis.
Langerhans cells present haptens to T cells, producing a delayed hypersensitivity reaction 48 to 72 hours after each exposure to the allergen in question every single time
That is allergic contact dermatitis.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which factors contribute to seborrhoeic dermatitis, and where does it occur?
opts: Cutaneous microbiome dysbiosis, altered immune response and epidermal barrier dysfunction, affecting regions rich in sebaceous glands — scalp, face and upper trunk
Correct, and the lecture is explicit that the cause is incompletely understood. Dandruff is the non-inflammatory form.
A single fungal pathogen acting alone, affecting mainly the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet rather than the sebaceous areas of the skin
The cause is described as multifactorial and incompletely understood, and the distribution follows sebaceous glands.
Autoimmune T cell activation, affecting the elbows and knees
That distribution and mechanism belong to psoriasis.
Ultraviolet damage, affecting sun-exposed skin
That is actinic keratosis.

set2.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: What produces lichenification, and what changes occur in the tissue?
opts: Loss of melanocytes across a circumscribed area
That produces a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo.
Separation of the epidermis from the dermis with accumulation of fluid between the two layers, forming a large blister that lifts the surface away
That is a bulla.
Slowing of keratinocyte division with elastin degradation
That is atrophy, which thins rather than thickens the skin.
Long-term scratching or rubbing of a pruritic area in an itch-scratch cycle, producing hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis with solid, firm, thick plaques without scaling
Correct, and lichen simplex chronicus is the named condition.

set2.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: Which causes are given for bullae?
opts: Capillary rupture and thrombocytopenia
Those produce petechiae and purpura.
Androgen stimulation of sebaceous glands
That relates to sebum production rather than blister formation.
Mechanical factors, infections, toxins, chemical exposure and autoimmune reactions
Correct, with bullous impetigo as the bacterial example and bullous pemphigoid as the autoimmune one.
Increased melanin production and cumulative ultraviolet light exposure alone
Those produce pigmented macules rather than bullae.

set2.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: A patient has thick, leathery plaques on the neck and forearms with no scaling, after months of scratching. Which secondary lesion is this, mechanistically?
opts: Ulcer, arising from focal loss of both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it
There is no tissue loss described here; the tissue is thickened.
Atrophy, from slowed keratinocyte division
Atrophy thins the skin, and this description is of thickening.
Lichenification, from hyperplasia and hyperkeratosis driven by the itch-scratch cycle
Correct. The absence of scaling is what separates it from psoriasis, whose plaques do scale.
Scale, from desquamating stratum corneum
Scaling is specifically absent in the description given.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What are the growth phases of melanoma, in order?
opts: Vertical growth down into the dermis first, then radial spread within the epidermis afterwards once the tumour has thickened sufficiently to invade
This reverses the first two phases.
Inflammatory, proliferative, then remodelling
Those are the phases of wound healing.
Sensitization then elicitation
Those are the phases of allergic contact dermatitis.
Radial growth within the epidermis, then vertical growth penetrating the dermis, then increasing tumour thickness, then metastatic invasion of lymphatics and blood vessels
Correct. The shift from radial to vertical is the point at which depth begins to matter.

set2.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: What forms during the proliferative phase, and what is it made of?
opts: A fibrin haemostatic plug, over days 1 to 3
That is the inflammatory phase.
Type I collagen laid down in parallel bundles, over days 21 to one year of remodelling
That is remodelling.
Keratohyalin granules within the granular layer
That is normal epidermal maturation, not wound healing.
Granulation tissue, comprised of macrophages, fibroblasts and endothelial cells, over days 4 to 21
Correct. Those three cell types supply clearance, matrix and new vessels respectively.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the suspected mechanism of koilonychia?
opts: Impaired keratin synthesis associated with deficiency anaemia, weakening the nail plate into raised ridges that are thin and concave
Correct, and the lecture notes the exact pathophysiology is unknown.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal transverse grooves across the surface of the nail plate itself
That is Beau's lines.
Overgrowth of connective tissue producing an opaque nail
That is Terry's nails.
Incomplete keratinization producing white spots
That is leukonychia.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which epidermal layer forms the semi-impermeable barrier, and what is it made of?
opts: The papillary dermis, a thin superficial connective tissue layer
That is dermis rather than epidermis.
The stratum corneum, 20 to 30 layers of keratin and dead keratinocytes cemented together
Correct. That packing is what makes callused skin, and losing it is what makes barrier-defect conditions possible.
The stratum basale, a single layer of rapidly dividing columnar keratinocytes at the base
That is the germinative layer, not the barrier.
The stratum granulosum, 3 to 5 layers of diamond-shaped cells
Those cells contain keratohyalin but do not themselves form the barrier.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which protein deficiency contributes to atopic dermatitis, and what does it reflect?
opts: Insufficient collagen, reflecting fibroblast failure
Collagen loss relates to atrophy and ulceration rather than eczema.
Insufficient elastin, reflecting loss of recoil
Elastin degradation is part of atrophy.
Insufficient keratohyalin, reflecting loss of the granular layer
Loss of the stratum granulosum is described for psoriasis.
Insufficient filaggrin, reflecting a compromised epidermal barrier
Correct, alongside an overactive immune system and genetic, environmental and psychogenic factors.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the mechanism of urticaria?
opts: T cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity 48 to 72 hours after exposure
That is allergic contact dermatitis.
Dysplastic keratinocyte proliferation from ultraviolet damage
That is actinic keratosis.
Capillary rupture with extravasation of blood
That produces petechiae and purpura.
Mast cell degranulation releasing histamine, producing wheals
Correct, and it may be acute or chronic with a wide range of triggers.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What gives the spinous layer its alternative name of prickle cell layer?
opts: Keratohyalin granules that give the cells a rough and irregular outline when viewed on microscopy
Those granules define the granular layer above it.
Melanin granules transferred from melanocytes
Pigment transfer does not produce the spiny appearance.
Dead flattened keratinocytes packed into scales
That describes the stratum corneum.
Keratinocytes connected by intercellular connections called desmosomes, which form a spiny appearance
Correct. This layer also contains the dendritic and Langerhans cells that act as immune sentinels.

set2.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: What does an epidermal inclusion cyst arise from and contain?
opts: A sebaceous gland, and it contains only squalene
The stated origin is the hair follicle and the content is keratin.
A blood vessel, and it contains clotted blood
No such origin is described for this lesion.
A hair follicle, and it contains keratin
Correct. A cyst is an elevated, circumscribed, encapsulated lesion in the dermis or subcutaneous layer with liquid or semisolid contents.
A sweat gland, and it contains sodium and chloride
Eccrine sweat contains those, but the cyst described arises from a follicle.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: How do dermatophytes obtain nutrition, and in which layer do they typically live?
opts: They proliferate within the dermis, digesting collagen
The stated location is the stratum corneum, and the substrate is keratin.
Spores secrete keratinases and proteases to metabolise and digest keratin in skin, hair and nails, typically within the stratum corneum
Correct — Trichophyton, Microsporum and Epidermophyton are the three most common, and the annular patch with central clearing follows from this.
They invade epidermal basal cells through microabrasions and drive proliferation of the epidermis above them over time
That is human papillomavirus.
They release histamine from mast cells producing wheals
That is urticaria.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: How do eccrine and apocrine sweat glands differ in secretion and function?
opts: Eccrine secrete keratin and apocrine secrete melanin
Neither gland secretes either of those.

Eccrine open onto the skin surface and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling by evaporation; apocrine sit mainly in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids, functioning as scent glands
Correct. Body odour comes from bacterial degradation of apocrine sweat, not from the sweat itself.
Eccrine glands sit in the axilla and anogenital areas and secrete protein and fatty lipids; apocrine glands open onto the surface of the skin and secrete water and electrolytes for cooling the body
This reverses the two glands entirely.
Both secrete sebum, differing only in the body regions they occupy
Sebum is the product of the sebaceous glands, which are a third type.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Where do melanocytes normally sit, and what drives their malignant transformation?
opts: Within the stratum corneum, transformed by keratinase digestion
That describes dermatophyte behaviour, not melanocyte biology.
In the reticular layer of the dermis, transformed by dysregulation of the fibroblasts that reside within it over a long period of time
Fibroblast dysregulation is the keloid mechanism.
In the basal layer, transformed by Hedgehog pathway activation
Hedgehog activation is the basal cell carcinoma mechanism.
At the dermal-epidermal junction, with ultraviolet light and oxidative stress damaging melanocyte DNA and leading to uninhibited growth
Correct, and the risk is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: How is melanoma risk inherited, according to the lecture?
opts: As an autosomal dominant trait with variable penetrance
Correct, though ultraviolet light and oxidative stress remain the primary driving factor.
As an autosomal recessive trait with complete penetrance
Neither the pattern nor the penetrance matches.
As an X-linked trait
No such inheritance is described.
It is entirely environmental with no inherited component
An inherited component is described explicitly.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: A patient reacts to a nickel earring 48 to 72 hours after wearing it. Which mechanism does the delay reflect?
opts: Viral proliferation within basal keratinocytes
That is verrucae vulgaris.
Delayed hypersensitivity requiring T cell migration after re-exposure to a hapten previously presented by Langerhans cells
Correct. The delay is the time the cellular response takes, which is what distinguishes it from an immediate mast cell reaction.
An immediate immunoglobulin E-mediated mast cell degranulation occurring upon the very first contact with the metal
That reaction occurs within minutes and produces wheals.
Direct chemical injury requiring no prior exposure
That is irritant contact dermatitis, which does not require sensitization.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What causes Beau's lines, and what are they associated with?
opts: Increased capillary density, associated with lung disease
That is clubbing.
Impaired keratin synthesis, associated with deficiency anaemia
That is koilonychia.
A halt of keratin production producing horizontal or transverse grooves, associated with illness, stress, injury to the nail and malnourishment
Correct — the groove marks the period during which the nail stopped being made.
Overgrowth of connective tissue within the nail bed, associated with chronic liver disease and with diabetes mellitus in particular
That is Terry's nails.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which skin cancer is described as the most common malignancy in humans, and how does it behave?
opts: Actinic keratosis, which is by far the most common malignancy occurring in human beings
Actinic keratosis is a precancer rather than a malignancy.
Basal cell carcinoma, slow growing and rarely metastasising, typically on the head and neck
Correct. Squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common.
Squamous cell carcinoma, rapidly metastasising
Squamous cell carcinoma is second most common.
Melanoma, slow growing and rarely metastasising
Melanoma progresses through radial to vertical growth and can metastasise.

set2.io: Objective d — Molecular mechanisms of common dermatological conditions
set2.q: What produces Terry's nails, and what conditions is it associated with?
opts: Overgrowth of connective tissue in the nail bed, associated with aging, liver disease, congestive heart failure or diabetes
Correct — the nail is opaque except for a dark band at the tip.
Increased capillary density together with vascular endothelial growth factor release into the tissue locally over time
That is clubbing.
Impaired keratin synthesis with deficiency anaemia
That is koilonychia.
Temporary incomplete keratinization at the nail bed
That is leukonychia.

set2.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: Why does an ulcer scar while an erosion generally does not?
opts: An ulcer destroys collagen in the dermis, so healing must lay down new collagen; an erosion spares the dermal-epidermal junction and the dermis beneath it
Correct. Scarring is a dermal repair process, so a lesion confined above the junction has nothing to scar.
An ulcer is infected and an erosion is sterile
Infection is not what defines either lesion.
An ulcer is larger, and size alone determines scarring
Depth rather than size is the operative difference.
An ulcer involves a loss of melanocytes from the basal layer which cannot be reversed once it has occurred in the tissue at any point afterwards
Melanocyte loss produces hypopigmentation and is not the ulcer mechanism.

set2.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: What is the tissue basis of a papule?
opts: Separation of epidermis from dermis with fluid accumulation
That is a bulla.
Focal loss of the epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction beneath it
That is an erosion, and it is a secondary lesion.
Hyperplasia of the epidermis with hyperkeratosis, plus inflammation and dense collagen fibres in the dermis
Correct, and seborrhoeic keratosis is the example given. A papule is elevated, solid, and under 5 millimetres.
Fluid containing inflammatory cells collecting within or beneath the epidermis
That is a vesicle.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What is the primary component of the dermis, which cell produces it, and what does it provide?
opts: Collagen, produced by fibroblasts, providing tensile strength
Correct, with elastic fibres of elastin and fibrillin providing elastic recoil and flexibility alongside it.
Keratin, produced by keratinocytes, providing an impermeable barrier
Keratin is an epidermal product.
Elastin, produced by mast cells, providing tensile strength
Elastin provides recoil rather than tensile strength, and mast cells do not produce it.
Melanin, produced by melanocytes, providing ultraviolet protection
Melanin is a pigment made in the epidermis.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: How often does the epidermis turn over, and what modifies that rate?
opts: Turnover ceases after adolescence
The epidermis renews throughout life.
Every 30 to 60 days, and turnover is more rapid in younger patients
Correct. Age-dependent turnover matters because it sets how quickly the epidermis can repair itself.
Every 24 to 48 hours, with no age dependence
That is far faster than the stated rate.
Every 6 to 12 months, and considerably more rapid in older patients
Both the interval and the direction of the age effect are wrong.

set2.io: Objective b — Pathophysiology of primary skin lesions
set2.q: What is the mechanism of a hypopigmented macule such as vitiligo, against a hyperpigmented one?
opts: Loss of melanocytes, against increased melanin production in the basal layer of the epidermis
Correct. Ephelides, café au lait spots and Mongolian spots are the hyperpigmented examples given.
Increased melanin production within the epidermis, as against loss of melanocytes entirely
This reverses the two mechanisms.
Capillary rupture with blood deposition in the dermis
That is the mechanism of petechiae and purpura.
Dilatation and thinning of superficial dermal vessels
That is telangiectasia.

set2.io: Objective c — Pathophysiology of secondary skin lesions
set2.q: What is the tissue distinction between an erosion and an ulcer?
opts: An erosion is focal loss of epidermis that does not penetrate below the dermal-epidermal junction; an ulcer is focal loss of epidermis AND dermis, with destruction of collagen and infiltration of inflammatory cells
Correct. The junction is the boundary that separates them, and crossing it is what brings collagen destruction into play.
An erosion involves both the epidermis and the dermis beneath it; an ulcer is limited to the epidermis alone and spares the dermal-epidermal junction entirely, so it never destroys collagen at all
This reverses the two.
An erosion is fluid-filled and an ulcer is solid
Neither is a fluid-filled lesion.
An erosion is a primary lesion and an ulcer is a secondary lesion
Both are secondary lesions.
